interpretation_history.interpretation: The route-log record shows manual-read route completion at 88% versus a 95% target across 9200 manual-read accounts for Aug-Sep 2026, indicating a measurable shortfall in completed field meter reads during the dispute-surge period.

The CRM record shows dispute ticket response times (median 1.6 days, p90 2.8 days) are already inside the 3.0-day SLA across 2440 tickets, so handling speed/capacity is not currently breaching target even though ticket volume has surged. This weakens the premise that the surge is a response-speed problem solvable by an auto-answering agent, and redirects attention to why bills are wrong in the first place.

The CRM record confirms the stakeholder's framing of magnitude: dispute tickets held near 600/month in June-July 2026 then jumped to roughly double (1180-1260) in August-September 2026, corroborating that a real surge occurred coincident with the dispute-surge period, though it is silent on root cause.

The billing-db record shows 1240 disputed bills carried an ESTIMATED read and 1785 carried an ACTUAL (accepted) read, i.e. a majority (1785/3025) of disputed bills were not estimate-substituted at all. This weakens any causal story that routes disputes solely through estimate substitution from failed AMI exports or missed field reads, and points to a sizeable chunk of disputes stemming from something else in the billing path (e.g. tariff/calculation errors) that affects accepted-read bills too.

The billing-db tariff change log shows zero records, meaning no tariff change was logged in the queried period. This rules out a tariff-rate change as the trigger for wrong bills, narrowing (but not eliminating) the billing-calculation-error explanation for disputes on accepted-read bills.

release_summary.summary: The customer-service request (CL-01) to build an AI agent that auto-answers tickets and auto-fixes "whatever causes wrong bills" was tested against evidence rather than taken at face value. Ticket response times are within SLA (E-02), so the surge is not a response-speed problem; instead, dispute volume roughly doubled from ~600 to ~1260/month since August (E-03), and a majority of the 3025 disputed bills (1785) carry an accepted ACTUAL meter read, not an estimated one (E-04) -- pointing to a billing-import correctness defect (H-BILLING-RULE-CHANGE, supported) rather than AMI/field read failures (both rejected). For the smaller estimated-read subset, most bills had valid AMI reads that were rejected at billing import for high consumption (E-12), not missing exports or field reads. The release (RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION, no holds) covers the rule-change-log query, the disputed-bill read-type cross-reference, and the field route completion diagnosis -- without any automated bill writes or route-dispatch changes, respecting K-BILLWRITE and K-DISPATCH. The underlying DEFINE gate was only a CONDITIONAL_PASS: the exact faulty billing rule was never pinpointed (VOB-U-RULE-CHANGE-SPECIFICS remains open, deferred outside this release's scope). The release record also surfaces, without resolving, an internal inconsistency: it cites mdms-export as still degraded/access-pending to justify excluding AMI-read verification, while other state fields show that access issue resolved, the tool healthy, and a successful mdms-export query (E-12) already executed. Several further limitations are carried forward: no automated bill corrections, uncertain billing-config tool health, unverified field-shortage causal contribution (with a stakeholder incentive bias noted), unknown data-handoff validity, and an inability to process the full batch of already-wrong bills within budget.
key_points: The original request (CL-01, from SH-CS) framed the dispute surge as a ticket-handling speed problem solvable by an auto-answer/auto-fix AI agent; this framing was rejected because ticket response times are within SLA (E-02/F-02) despite the volume surge, so handling speed is not the bottleneck (H-RESPONSE-SPEED-FRAMING: REJECTED).

The root problem was established as a billing-import correctness defect: dispute volume roughly doubled from ~600 to ~1260/month starting August (E-03/F-03), but a majority of disputed bills (1785 of 3025) carry an accepted ACTUAL read rather than an ESTIMATED one (E-04/F-04), implicating billing-import logic rather than just estimate substitution.

output.summary: The customer-service request (CL-01) to build an AI agent that auto-answers tickets and auto-fixes "whatever causes wrong bills" was tested against evidence rather than taken at face value. Ticket response times are within SLA (E-02), so the surge is not a response-speed problem; instead, dispute volume roughly doubled from ~600 to ~1260/month since August (E-03), and a majority of the 3025 disputed bills (1785) carry an accepted ACTUAL meter read, not an estimated one (E-04) -- pointing to a billing-import correctness defect (H-BILLING-RULE-CHANGE, supported) rather than AMI/field read failures (both rejected). For the smaller estimated-read subset, most bills had valid AMI reads that were rejected at billing import for high consumption (E-12), not missing exports or field reads. The release (RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION, no holds) covers the rule-change-log query, the disputed-bill read-type cross-reference, and the field route completion diagnosis -- without any automated bill writes or route-dispatch changes, respecting K-BILLWRITE and K-DISPATCH. The underlying DEFINE gate was only a CONDITIONAL_PASS: the exact faulty billing rule was never pinpointed (VOB-U-RULE-CHANGE-SPECIFICS remains open, deferred outside this release's scope). The release record also surfaces, without resolving, an internal inconsistency: it cites mdms-export as still degraded/access-pending to justify excluding AMI-read verification, while other state fields show that access issue resolved, the tool healthy, and a successful mdms-export query (E-12) already executed. Several further limitations are carried forward: no automated bill corrections, uncertain billing-config tool health, unverified field-shortage causal contribution (with a stakeholder incentive bias noted), unknown data-handoff validity, and an inability to process the full batch of already-wrong bills within budget.
